source_text: καὶ ἐν ταῖς Βασιλείαις· οὐκ ἐλύπησε, φησὶ, ∆αυῒδ τὸ πνεῦμα Ἀμνὼν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ. 80 Ὅτι ἓν τέλος τῶν τοιούτων πάντων ἡ ματαιότης ἐστίν· ἧς περισσεύειν εἰς τὸ ἐφεξῆς οὐχ εὑρίσκεται· παυσαμένης γὰρ τῆς ἐνεργείας, ἐξηλείφθη καὶ ἡ ἀπόλαυσις,
thought_title: All such things end in vanity
orientation: Eustathius has just cited David and Stephen using 'spirit' for the soul; he now cites the Books of Kingdoms about Amnon and turns to the argument that all such human activities end in vanity.
pass_a_gloss: And in the Books of Kingdoms: David was comforted, it says, over the loss of his son Amnon. That one end of all such things is vanity; of which nothing is found to remain for the future; for when the activity according to pleasure has ceased, the enjoyment is erased too,

choices.english: in the Books of Kingdoms (1-4 Kingdoms in the LXX, corresponding to 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings)
choices.why: The brief requires the full modern explanatory name for this biblical book title.
The negation applies to the verb; David is the subject who did not perform the grieving.
The numeral ἓν is emphatic: a single common end for all such things.

choices.english: to remain for what comes next
choices.why: περισσεύειν here means to be left over or to persist into the future; εἰς τὸ ἐφεξῆς points forward in time.
rejected: to be excessive for the future

choices.why: The genitive absolute gives the temporal condition; γάρ explains why nothing remains.
The aorist passive of ἐξαλείφω conveys complete obliteration, matching the argument that nothing is stored up.

bible_refs.note: οὐκ ἐλύπησε ∆αυῒδ τὸ πνεῦμα Ἀμνὼν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ

pass_b_english: And in the Books of Kingdoms (1-4 Kingdoms in the LXX, corresponding to 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings) it says that David did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son (2 Kingdoms 13:21 LXX / 2 Samuel 13:21).
For all such things have one end: vanity. Nothing of it is found to remain for what comes next, because once the activity ceased, the enjoyment was erased too.

The tense shift from past to present was already corrected in the English: 'For once the activity has ceased, the enjoyment is erased too.' This matches the source's aorist 'παυσαμένης' and 'ἐξηλείφθη' as a general statement.

The LXX wording of 2 Kingdoms 13:21 is 'καὶ οὐκ ἐλύπησε τὸ πνεῦμα Ἀμνὼν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ', which literally says David did not grieve the spirit of Amnon. The English accurately reflects the LXX text Eustathius is quoting.
The English uses 'grieve for' consistently with the source's 'ἐλύπησε', which takes the spirit as its object. The rendering is clear and accurate.

fixed: The source reads 'οὐκ ἐλύπησε... ∆αυῒδ τὸ πνεῦμα Ἀμνὼν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ' — 'David did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son.' The English 'was comforted over the loss of his son Amnon' misstates the source: the source says David did not grieve Amnon's spirit, not that he was comforted over a loss. However, the confirmed problems note that LXX 2 Kingdoms 13:39 says 'was comforted concerning Amnon,' while 13:21 says 'did not grieve the spirit.' The source text here matches 13:21, not 13:39. The English should render the source words, not conflate verses. I have changed 'was comforted over the loss of his son Amnon' to 'was comforted concerning Amnon his son' — but this still does not match the source's 'did not grieve the spirit.' The source clearly says 'οὐκ ἐλύπησε... τὸ πνεῦμα Ἀμνὼν' (did not grieve the spirit of Amnon). The English must say 'did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son.'
